newsitem.title: USA: Blue chips fall on profit-taking; interest rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Blue chips fall on profit-taking; interest rate fears.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Wednesday on profit-taking after setting two consecutive records as Wall Street worried about rising long-term interest rates.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 51.18 points at 6,549.48, one day after finishing above the 6,600 level for the first time. The Dow also set a record on Monday.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,272 to 1,238 on active volume of 556 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"What's happened in the last few days is stocks have lost their cushion," said Douglas Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at J.P. Morgan. "With bond yields backing up the way they have, I would characterise stocks as fully valued."

Concerns about interest rates, which resurfaced in force after a surprisingly strong National Association of Purchasing Management report last week, have intensified ahead of two key economic reports due later this week -- the Producer Price Index on Thursday and monthly employment figures on Friday.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 5/8 point, or $6.25 per $1,000 face value, and its yield rose to 6.84 percent from 6.79 percent Tuesday. The yield moves in the opposite direction to the price.
While stocks have shown increased volatility this week, the market has essentially run in place. The Dow's loss on Wednesday left it virtually unchanged from its opening on Monday.

"The market is waiting for some event to give it a catalyst," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "I think the best candidate will be the employment data on Friday but it could come from the PPI."

A group of economists surveyed by Reuters expect, an overall 0.3 percent rise in December producer prices. The so-called "core" rate, which excludes the volatile food and energy components, is expected to rise by 0.1 percent.

In a pattern becoming almost routine lately in stocks, the session was marked by a wave of computerized programme trades, seven over the day, according to Birinyi Associates, a firm that tracks programme trading.
The stocks of major money centre banks fared well, despite the latest jump in long-term interest rates.

Analysts said the gains by banks came amid expectations of strong earnings reports next week. Also, the banking industry got a boost when the Federal Reserve proposed removing many barriers to banks' activities in the securities industry.
Chase Manhattan Corp. rose 7/8 to 87-5/8 and J.P. Morgan & Co. gained 1-1/8 to 99-3/8.

Templeton Russia Fund, the only NYSE listed fund that trades exclusively in Russian companies, fell 1-1/8 to 23 on news that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had been hospitalized after showing signs of pneumonia.
Loewen Group Inc. fell 4-1/8 to 36-3/4 after Service Corp. International withdrew a $2.9 billion hostile takeover offer for the funeral services company. Service Corp. rose 1-3/4 to 29-3/8.
Shiva Corp. lost almost half its value, plunging 15-5/8 to 19-1/4 after the data communications equipment maker said its fourth-quarter earnings would be well below analysts' estimates.
Netscape Communications Corp. tumbled 10-7/8 to 47-7/8 after Deutsche Morgan Grenfell downgraded the company.
The Nasdaq Composite index lost 7.38 points to 1,320.35.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 4.82 to 748.41. The American Stock Exchange index was up 1.09 to 576.72.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.65 to 395.25. The average share was down 17 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,269.642 down 29.505 or 0.40 percent.
